strengths: Well-motivated and novel framing: representing the latent manifold as an implicit submanifold via a learned projection, so that all geometric operators (geodesics, exponential map) are computed directly in the low-dimensional latent space rather than on the high-dimensional data manifold.

Principled projection learning: minimizing the denoising objective (Eq. 12) yields a Gaussian-weighted barycenter with a clean minimizer characterization, extending the Alain & Bengio (2014) denoising-autoencoder result to latent manifolds of unknown codimension.

The discrete geodesic calculus is grounded in an established, provably convergent framework (Rumpf & Wirth 2015), and the use of an augmented Lagrangian method tailored to inexact constraints (Algorithm 1) is a practically sensible choice for imperfect representations.

Broad empirical demonstration across synthetic (torus) and real settings (SCAPE discrete shells, CMU motion capture with SVAE, rotating-cow images with a low-bending/low-distortion autoencoder, and Pose-NDF), plus a distance-function variant that avoids requiring normal information.

Reproducibility is generally good: appendix gives architectures, hyperparameters, optimizer settings, σ values, and the authors reuse publicly available pretrained models (Braunsmann et al. 2024; Pose-NDF) and published implementations (GOAST).
Limitations are discussed honestly (σ-dependent accuracy, O(σ²)/O(σ) defect, missing normal information for the distance-function case), and concrete future directions are given.
weaknesses: Evaluation is almost entirely qualitative (visual sequences of decoded shapes). No quantitative metrics are reported on the real-data experiments (e.g., endpoint/geodesic-energy error, distance-to-manifold, self-intersection counts, or runtime), so the claimed advantages cannot be measured.

No comparison against the most relevant prior methods that also compute geodesics on autoencoder latent spaces (Shao et al. 2018; Chen et al. 2018; Arvanitidis et al. 2018, 2021). Without such baselines it is impossible to judge whether the proposed approach improves over the state of the art rather than merely reproducing it.

The central claim that the method is robust to imperfect implicit representations is asserted rather than demonstrated. The cited convergence results (Rumpf & Wirth 2015) hold for the exact ζ; the effect of using the approximate ζ_σ on geodesic accuracy is not analyzed or quantified, and the discrete exponential uses a plain penalty on ζ(z_k)=0 rather than the augmented Lagrangian.

No computational-cost or scaling analysis, despite reduced-order efficiency being a primary motivation. The discrete exponential requires solving a nonlinear system with BFGS at every step, and behavior with respect to K, latent dimension, and codimension is not discussed.

Choice of σ and network capacity is heuristic ('rule-of-thumb'); sensitivity is only examined on the toy torus, and no principled selection procedure is provided for real latent manifolds with unknown sampling density.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the two core ingredients—the denoising-based projection (Alain & Bengio 2014) and the time-discrete geodesic calculus (Rumpf & Wirth 2015)—are existing, and the integration with inexact-constraint handling is not analyzed in depth.

Some conclusions are confounded by design choices: the claim that geodesics 'avoid self-intersections more effectively' relies on discarding self-intersecting training pairs, which is a data-curation step rather than a property of the geodesic calculus itself.

Failure modes when the latent manifold is not a clean low-dimensional submanifold (e.g., noisy or high-codimension latent spaces) are not characterized, and no diagnostic is offered for when the implicit representation is too inaccurate to be used.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and difficult problem: equipping autoencoder latent spaces with practical Riemannian operators for geodesic interpolation and extrapolation, with potential impact in shape analysis and generative modeling.

The implicit representation ζ(z)=z−Π(z) with a learned approximate projection is encoder-independent and can accommodate multiple metrics (Euclidean, pullback, distance-based), which is a flexible conceptual framework.
Adapts time-discrete variational geodesic calculus (Rumpf & Wirth) to latent manifolds and provides concrete augmented-Lagrangian and discrete-exponential algorithms.

Demonstrates the pipeline across several settings: torus toy example with ground-truth comparison, discrete shells/SCAPE, CMU motion capture with SVAE, rotating-cow image data, and Pose-NDF distance function.
Includes useful implementation details and parameter studies in the appendix (projection training, augmented Lagrangian, data generation, network architectures).
Qualitative results suggest geodesic paths can avoid artifacts such as self-intersections and implausible poses relative to linear interpolation in latent space.
The paper acknowledges some limitations and points to future directions, such as connecting projection-based and distance-based representations, adaptive σ, and latent distributions.
weaknesses: No quantitative evaluation: all real-data experiments rely on visual plausibility; there are no metrics for geodesic accuracy, path energy, endpoint error, reconstruction error, self-intersection rate, or runtime.

No baselines beyond linear interpolation and Euclidean metric; no comparison to prior latent-space geometry methods such as Arvanitidis et al. (2018, 2021, 2022), Sun et al. (2025), Chen et al. (2018), or Shao et al. (2018), despite directly related work.

Theoretical claims are not established: the cited convergence result for discrete geodesic calculus assumes an exact smooth manifold and a suitable W approximating squared distance. There is no convergence or error analysis for the learned approximate projection ζ_σ or for the inexact augmented Lagrangian. The claim of robustness to imperfect implicit representations is only qualitatively suggested on a toy torus.

Strong assumptions limit generality: the method requires either known Riemannian distances on the data manifold or a near-isometric autoencoder. General autoencoders with unknown or irregular metrics are not handled. The conclusion admits this requirement.

Projection learning is heuristic and underspecified: the denoising objective uses a single noise sample per data point per optimization step; no approximation-error bounds are given, and the stated defects O(σ^2) in the interior and O(σ) near the boundary are not propagated through the geodesic calculus. Selection of σ appears manual and problem-specific.

The discrete exponential is numerically fragile; Fig. 3 shows exponential divergence of trajectories, and no stabilization or quantification of this effect is provided. The augmented-Lagrangian scheme involves underdetermined multipliers and penalty heuristics that are not rigorously justified.

Experiments contain potential confounds: training discards shapes with self-intersections, which may artificially encourage geodesics to avoid self-intersections; the SVAE experiment ignores the nondeterministic encoder/decoder and KL term without comparing to Arvanitidis et al. (2022) on the same data.
No ablation in the main experiments for K, σ, projection architecture, metric choice, or augmented-Lagrangian parameters. The parameter study is limited to the toy torus.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code release or computational details such as seeds, hardware, runtimes, or hyperparameter search are provided. Algorithm 1 contains inconsistencies/typos (e.g., L^α vs L^a, tolerance and multiplier updates).
Presentation issues: notation is inconsistent (R^i vs R^l, ζ vs ζ_σ, W_M vs W_E), some equations and algorithm steps are unclear, and the qualitative figures are small and difficult to assess.
The paper lacks a dedicated limitations section and does not discuss failure cases, computational cost, scalability, or broader ethical/societal impact beyond brief mentions.

Originality and significance are limited: the contribution mainly combines existing discrete geodesic calculus with a denoising-based projection. There is no new theoretical insight and no evidence that the approach scales to high-dimensional latent spaces or large datasets.

strengths: Addresses an important open problem: equipping autoencoder latent spaces with usable Riemannian geometry and practical geodesic interpolation/extrapolation operators.

Introduces a clean implicit representation of the latent manifold via a learned approximate projection trained with a denoising objective, which is autoencoder-agnostic and supports different Riemannian metrics.

Develops a time-discrete geodesic calculus adapted to imperfect implicit representations, with augmented Lagrangian and BFGS algorithms for interpolation and the discrete exponential map, grounded in the Rumpf--Wirth variational discretization framework.

Demonstrates the approach on a diverse set of examples: synthetic torus, discrete shells/SCAPE, motion capture with an SVAE, rotating-object images, and the Pose-NDF distance function; qualitative results indicate geodesics avoid artifacts and follow the latent manifold better than linear interpolation.
Reproducibility is generally good: the appendix provides dataset details, network architectures, hyperparameters, training procedures, and references to public datasets and pretrained models.
The paper is well motivated and positions itself clearly relative to shape analysis, latent-space geometry, and neural implicit representations.
weaknesses: Evaluation is almost entirely qualitative. There are no quantitative metrics for geodesic accuracy, manifold adherence, reconstruction error, distance preservation, or runtime, and the only main baseline is linear interpolation. Comparisons to prior latent geodesic methods such as Arvanitidis et al., Shao et al., Chen et al., or Sun et al. (2025) are missing.

The theoretical convergence guarantees apply to exact smooth manifolds and exact distance approximations, but the method in practice uses a learned approximate projection and inexact constraints. The claimed robustness to inaccurate implicit representations is supported mainly by a toy torus experiment and is not analyzed quantitatively for the real-data experiments.

The choice of the projection scale sigma and its interaction with sampling density, noise level, and manifold curvature is not resolved. The paper notes a trade-off between smoothing and projection accuracy but offers no principled selection criterion for real applications.

Several experiments rely on ground-truth distances or metrics on the data manifold (e.g., discrete shell distance, SO(3) distance, known image rotations), which are not generally available in unsupervised latent-space settings. This limits the applicability of the method as presented.
Geodesic extrapolation via the discrete exponential map is numerically unstable, as shown in Figure 3, but stability, step-size dependence, and error accumulation are not quantitatively studied.

For probabilistic autoencoders, the method ignores the nondeterministic encoder/decoder and samples a single point per vMF distribution. The KL/Fisher--Rao alternative is mentioned but not evaluated, leaving the distributional geometry of VAE latent spaces underexplored.

Presentation has minor technical and notational issues: Algorithm 1 contains inconsistencies (e.g., omega^k vs omega^j, multiplier update notation), there is at least one typo (ambient R^i), and key numerical details such as K values and runtime are not reported in the main text.
There is no explicit limitations section; limitations are discussed only briefly in the conclusion and future-work discussion.

strengths: Introduces a principled implicit representation of latent manifolds via a learned approximate projection from a denoising objective, enabling access to normal/tangent information and handling arbitrary codimension without requiring an explicit parametrization.

Develops a time-discrete variational geodesic calculus on this implicit representation, including algorithms for geodesic interpolation and exponential maps, built on established convergence results for exact representations.

Supports multiple Riemannian metrics (Euclidean, pullback, data-space distance, KL/Fisher-Rao) and is compatible with different autoencoder types (isometric autoencoder, SVAE, low-bending/low-distortion autoencoder, and distance-function manifolds such as Pose-NDF).

Provides a substantial appendix with implementation details, parameter studies, and comparisons to Stochman, LAND, and uncertainty-regularized VAE methods, adding useful context and practical evidence.

Demonstrates qualitative improvements over linear interpolation and some baselines on synthetic and real datasets, including torus geodesics, discrete shells, motion capture, image rotations, and human pose manifolds.
The framework is largely independent of the underlying autoencoder and can leverage pretrained models, suggesting potential for reduced-order shape analysis and geometry-aware generative modeling.
weaknesses: The central claim of robustness against imperfect implicit representations lacks quantitative error analysis. Convergence guarantees apply to exact smooth implicit functions and distance approximations, not to the learned approximate projection, and there are no bounds on how projection error propagates to geodesics or exponential maps.

The experimental evaluation is largely qualitative visual comparison. Apart from the torus toy example, there are no standard quantitative metrics for geodesic accuracy, path energy error, endpoint distance, or downstream task performance on real data.

Comparisons to related methods are mostly in the appendix and are sometimes qualitative or runtime-only. Some baseline failures (e.g., Arvanitidis et al. 2022 not converging) may depend on tuning, and there is no comparison to recent implicit-manifold methods such as Sun et al. (2025).

Scalability to high-dimensional latent spaces is not demonstrated. Projection-based experiments use latent dimensions up to 24, while the 84-dimensional example uses a distance function rather than the learned projection. The augmented Lagrangian optimizes K*l variables, which may be expensive for modern large latent spaces.

Projection learning is sensitive to the choice of sigma and may be unreliable near boundaries or where the codimension varies. The paper acknowledges O(sigma) boundary error but does not provide adaptive or boundary-aware handling.

For variational autoencoders, the method largely ignores encoder/decoder stochasticity by using means or single samples, which may discard geometric information and limit applicability to probabilistic latent manifolds.

The term 'geodesic calculus' is somewhat overstated: the paper provides interpolation and exponential maps but not parallel transport, curvature, or other calculus operations, which are left to future work.

Presentation has minor issues: some equations and algorithm pseudocode contain typos or unclear notation (e.g., missing norm in the augmented Lagrangian definition, index inconsistencies), and there is no dedicated limitations section.

Reproducibility could be strengthened by releasing code and exact data-generation scripts. While hyperparameters are detailed, full replication requires assembling external code, pretrained models, and datasets.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent and well-motivated framework that connects an implicit (zero-level-set) representation of the latent manifold with a variational time-discrete geodesic calculus, enabling both geodesic interpolation and exponential-map extrapolation on latent manifolds.

The use of a denoising-objective projection (following Alain & Bengio, 2014) to obtain the implicit representation is elegant and, importantly, is independent of the specific autoencoder and compatible with several Riemannian metrics (Euclidean, pullback, KL/Fisher-Rao).

The framework is demonstrated on a genuinely diverse set of settings (discrete shells/SCAPE, SVAE motion capture, low-bending/low-distortion image autoencoder, Pose-NDF distance field), and the qualitative decoded sequences do appear more plausible than linear interpolation.

The manuscript is generally well written, the Riemannian background is clearly laid out, and the limitations section and appendices (implementation of the augmented Lagrangian, projection parameter study) are reasonably detailed.
The work addresses a real and non-trivial gap: equipping autoencoder latent spaces with practically usable geometric operators, which most prior work leaves implicit.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence is almost entirely qualitative. Section 5 consists of side-by-side decoded image/pose sequences with no quantitative metric of geodesic accuracy, constraint violation, or adherence to the latent distribution. For a method paper this is a serious evidential gap; even simple checks (e.g., how closely the discrete geodesic satisfies the geodesic ODE, or path-length vs. a ground-truth/reference distance) are absent for the real-data experiments.

The core methodological ingredients are largely borrowed: the time-discrete geodesic calculus is Rumpf & Wirth (2015), the projection learning is Alain & Bengio (2014), and the optimizer is a standard augmented Lagrangian method. The novelty is essentially the combination and its application to latent manifolds, which limits the originality relative to the strong claims made.

The paper's headline claim—robustness to imperfect implicit representations ζ_σ = id − Π_σ (which does not actually vanish on Z)—is not rigorously supported. The cited convergence result (Rumpf & Wirth, Cor. 4.10) assumes a smooth manifold, a Lipschitz metric, and W approximating dist² to O(dist³); these assumptions are violated by the inexact constraint, and no convergence or error analysis is provided for the ζ_σ case. The robustness is argued only anecdotally from figures.

The comparisons to prior work (Stochman, LAND, Arvanitidis et al. 2022/2018) are relegated to the appendix, are mostly qualitative, and appear constructed to favor the proposed method. Statements such as the baseline optimization 'does not converge' and 'leaves the data manifold' are asserted without supporting numbers, and the reported timings/energies are not a fair or systematic benchmark. The comparison would need controlled, quantitative protocol to be persuasive.

The evaluation of how the projection quality (σ, sampling density, network size) propagates to geodesic accuracy is confined to the toy torus (Fig. 11). It is unclear how sensitive the downstream geodesic calculus is to the O(σ²)/O(σ) defect of the learned projection in the real-data regimes that matter.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: no code release is mentioned, several experiments depend on expensive custom data generation (PGA on discrete shells, shell geodesics for isometry pairs) and on pretrained external models, which makes independent reproduction difficult.

Applicability is narrower than the framing suggests. As the conclusion concedes, the method requires either fast distance evaluation on the data manifold or a (near-)isometric latent embedding, and the approach is essentially demonstrated on problems that already come from shape analysis with known ground-truth geometry—raising the question of whether the 'learning' component is doing real work or whether a classical shape-space computation would suffice.

For an ICML audience the framing is thin: much of the technical content is geometry-processing machinery, and the machine-learning contribution (a learned projection) is not benchmarked against alternatives (e.g., deriving Π from a distance function d, multi-scale/adaptive σ), leaving the practical advantage over existing latent-geometry methods unestablished.

strengths: Soundness: The paper develops a coherent mathematical framework for treating latent manifolds as implicit submanifolds via a learned projection Pi_sigma, with a principled denoising objective whose minimizer is a Gaussian-weighted barycenter. The discrete geodesic calculus builds on established variational time discretization (Rumpf & Wirth, 2015) and gives practical augmented-Lagrangian algorithms for geodesic interpolation and exponential maps.

Originality/significance: The implicit representation of latent manifolds with unknown codimension is a fresh and useful perspective. It decouples geodesic computation from the autoencoder architecture and supports multiple metrics (Euclidean, pullback, manifold distance, KL), enabling interpolation and extrapolation on real shape, motion, image, and pose data.

Presentation: The main text is generally clear and well organized, with helpful figures and a detailed appendix covering hyperparameters, data generation, and comparisons to Stochman, uncertainty-regularized VAEs, and LAND.
Reproducibility: The appendix gives network architectures, training schedules, data sources, and hyperparameters; public datasets and pretrained models are used, which supports reproducibility.
Limitations/ethics: The authors honestly discuss dependence on sigma, sampling density, and the need for fast distance evaluation or near-isometric embeddings. No major ethical concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Evaluation is largely qualitative on real data. The main results compare geodesic interpolation to linear interpolation, but do not report quantitative metrics of geodesic accuracy, manifold adherence, or interpolation quality against ground-truth geodesics (e.g., SCAPE shape-space geodesics or SO(3)^m distances). Stronger baselines (Arvanitidis et al., 2022; LAND; Stochman) are mostly relegated to appendix toy comparisons.

The central claim of robustness to imperfect implicit representations is not supported by a formal error analysis. The cited convergence guarantees assume exact smooth zeta and exact constraint satisfaction; the paper argues empirically that the augmented Lagrangian works for inexact zeta_sigma, but does not bound how errors in Pi_sigma propagate to discrete geodesics or the exponential map.

Key hyperparameter sigma is problem-dependent and manually selected; no principled or adaptive selection procedure is provided. The projection defect O(sigma^2) in the interior and O(sigma) near boundaries could affect manifolds with boundary, yet boundary handling is not analyzed or ablated.

Scalability is not thoroughly assessed. The method optimizes over K*l latent variables and requires training an additional projection network; experiments use moderate latent dimensions (10-24, plus 84 for Pose-NDF). Runtime and scaling with latent dimension, sample size, and path resolution K are not analyzed.

The SVAE experiment simplifies the probabilistic geometry by using decoder means and ignoring the KL/Fisher-Rao metric, despite the SVAE's motivation being hyperspherical latent geometry. No ablation justifies this simplification or compares to the full probabilistic metric.
No code release for the proposed method is mentioned, and several parameters are problem-dependent; combined with the lack of quantitative benchmarks, full reproducibility remains partial.
